title: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum
hook: night one: seeds in a clay dish, a pot of water, and a festival that works like a course taken in order

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Lalita Sahasranama closed on Lalitambika, Lalita the mother. Tonight, the goddess's nine nights begin.
screen: `THE LAST WORD IS MOTHER.` → `THE NINE NIGHTS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: In some homes in North India, the first night of Navaratri starts with dirt. A shallow clay dish, a layer of soil, a handful of barley seeds pressed in. A pot of water is set beside it, or on it, with mango leaves and a coconut at its mouth, and a lamp is lit. Night by night, almost nothing seems to happen. Then something does: by the end of the festival, the dish is full of thin green shoots. Nine nights, and a lesson you can watch grow.
screen: `SOIL, SEEDS, A POT OF WATER.` → `NIGHT BY NIGHT.` → `A LESSON YOU CAN WATCH GROW.`

segments.voice: You met these nights on day eighty. Now, the nights taken in order. Navaratri means nine nights, and they belong to the goddess. There's more than one Navaratri in the year; the one this path keeps falls in autumn. And the Devi Mahatmya, read whole at the start of this year, points at that season. Near its end the goddess says, in paraphrase: at the great worship held in autumn, whoever hears this story of mine with devotion will be freed from troubles. So for some households the nights are also a reading plan, the Devi Mahatmya recited across them. Why call it a curriculum? The nights aren't nine copies of one evening. They come in order, like a course. In some places each night has its own form of the goddess, its own color, its own offerings. Families don't all keep it the same way, and regions differ a great deal: dancing in one place, a staircase of dolls in another, great images of Durga in another. But underneath, the shape repeats. You begin, you stay, and the staying does the work. One way of counting gives the first nights to Durga, the one who faces down whatever blocks the road. That makes night one the first day of school: you just show up and plant something. Nobody expects shoots tonight. The seed is sown so the coming nights have something to tend. The curriculum begins with a beginning, and trusts the rest to time.
screen: `NINE NIGHTS FOR THE GODDESS.` · `HEAR MY STORY IN AUTUMN.` · `IN ORDER, LIKE A COURSE.` · `NIGHT ONE: SHOW UP AND PLANT.` · then, large: `A BEGINNING, TRUSTED TO TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you'd like to grow over the next nine nights, not a resolution but a seed: a little more patience at dinner, ten minutes of reading, calling your grandmother. Hold it lightly, like a seed between two fingers, then set it down in good soil and leave it there. If you pray, you can offer it to the goddess on this first night, in your own words; if you don't, simply let it be planted.
Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Nine nights for the goddess, kept in order like a course. Night one: show up, and plant something.
Your line: Navaratri as a nine-night curriculum. Night one is for planting, not for judging. Night one, done.

howItsDone: In some North Indian homes the first day of Navaratri begins with ghatasthapana: a water pot is installed for the goddess and barley is sown in soil to sprout through the nine nights; elsewhere the first night opens with dance, a display of dolls, or recitation of the Devi Mahatmya.

notes: Devi Mahatmya 12 paraphrased: the goddess says that at the great annual worship in autumn, whoever hears this Mahatmya with devotion will be freed from troubles. Confirm verse (c. 12.11–12) and wording.

Ghatasthapana with barley (jau/jaware) sown and sprouting by the end: described as 'some homes in North India'; confirm the details (mango leaves, coconut, the dish placement) and that sprouting by the end is fair.
Spring (Chaitra) and autumn (Sharad) Navaratris are both kept; the script says only that there is more than one.
'In some places each night has its own form, color and offerings' — 'many' is general; confirm or soften.
1109 = night one, agreed with the 1112–1121 writer (who counts 1112 = night four). Only Durga's first stretch is introduced here; 1112 sets out the full three-by-three scheme.
